definition.text: Discounting is the arrangement in which someone who owes money pays a charge for the right to delay the payment for a set time.

facts.text: The discount is the gap between what is owed today and the larger amount that must be paid later to settle the debt.
Most people prefer money now to money later, because of mortality, impatience and salience effects.
A payment made in the future is worth less than the same payment today, because money in hand now could be banked to earn interest.
The debtor who delays is in effect compensating the creditor for the income the money could have earned by being invested meanwhile.
Most models assume the discount yield equals the return the money could earn in other assets of similar risk over the same period.
Discounting is tied to the time value of money: a payment has a different future value and present value.
Discounting turns a future payment into its present value, also called its discounted value.

definition.text: The discount rate is the rate at which the charge for delaying a payment must grow as the delay gets longer.

facts.text: The discount yield is the share of the original debt that must be paid to delay payment for one year.
In financial calculations the discount rate is usually set equal to the cost of capital.
The rate may be adjusted upward to allow for the risk that expected cash flows will not arrive.
Start-up firms are typically given higher discount rates than established companies, reflecting disadvantages such as hard-to-sell shares and few willing investors.
The capital asset pricing model builds a discount rate as the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity market risk premium.
The risk-free rate is the return from investing in risk-free securities such as government bonds.

definition.text: A discount factor is the number a future cash flow is multiplied by to get its present value.

facts.text: It is computed from a zero (spot) rate taken from a yield curve and the time in years until the cash flow.
Banks usually discount cash flows with daily compounding, because accrued interest on their assets can be re-lent every day.
For hand calculation, continuous compounding is sometimes a close enough approximation to daily compounding.
In dynamic decision models, impatience is represented by a discount factor between 0 and 1.

definition.text: Hyperbolic discounting is a model of how people devalue delayed rewards in which their choices are not consistent over time.

facts.text: Under hyperbolic discounting, value falls quickly over short early delays but more slowly over longer delays.
In an early study, people were indifferent between $15 now and $30 in 3 months, $60 in 1 year or $100 in 3 years: implied yearly discount rates fell from 277% to 139% to 63%.
By contrast, exponential discounting lowers value by a constant factor per unit of delay, so the discount rate stays the same.
Many people take $50 now over $100 in a year, yet almost everyone picks $100 in six years over $50 in five years, though it is the same trade-off.
Its key consequence is temporary preferences for smaller, sooner rewards over larger, later ones, so people make choices their future selves regret.
It is described by the discount factor g(D) = 1/(1 + kD), where D is the delay and k sets how strongly rewards are discounted.
Preference reversals were first found in rats and pigeons, so the effect does not depend on human culture.
It is one of the cornerstones of behavioral economics and has been used to study retirement saving, credit-card borrowing, addiction and procrastination.

title: Uncertain hazard as a source of hyperbolic discounting

definition.text: One explanation of hyperbolic discounting is that a future reward carries a risk of not arriving, and that risk is uncertain.

facts.text: A restaurateur offered $100,000 in sixty years instead of $50 today would reasonably discount it, since the payer or payee may have died.
If the hazard rate of losing the reward is unknown and given a prior distribution, the expected survival probability of the reward takes exactly the hyperbolic form.
Whether discounting future gains is rational, and at what rate, depends greatly on circumstances.

definition.text: Quasi-hyperbolic or beta-delta discounting is a discrete-time approximation of hyperbolic discounting proposed by Laibson in 1997.

facts.text: It uses two constants, beta and delta, each between 0 and 1, with delays counted in whole periods.
Rewards taken now are not discounted at all.
It keeps much of the mathematical convenience of exponential discounting while capturing the main feature of hyperbolic discounting.

title: Criticism of hyperbolic discounting

definition.text: Researchers have proposed several alternative explanations for the non-exponential discounting that hyperbolic models describe.

facts.text: Daniel Read's subadditive discounting holds that discounting over a delay grows when the delay is split into smaller intervals.
The most obvious objection is that many people learn to choose consistently over time in most situations.
A 2014 paper criticised studies for relying mostly on university students and concluding too quickly that the hyperbolic model is correct.
Human experiments often show wide differences between subjects.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether hyperbolic discounting, a similarity heuristic or subadditive discounting best explains observed choices.

title: Social discount rate

definition.text: The social discount rate is the discount rate used to value money spent on public or social projects.

facts.text: It puts a present value on costs and benefits that come later, and it is critical when costs and benefits are spread unevenly over a long time.
It is used to value projects such as highways, schools or environmental protection, where future costs include maintenance and future benefits include reduced pollution.
A higher social discount rate makes a social project less likely to be funded.
A small rise in the rate can matter enormously for benefits far in the future.
The US Office of Management and Budget recommends about 7% as a pretax return on private investment, while HM Treasury sets 3.5% for the UK public sector.
Developed nations typically use lower rates (3–7%) than developing nations (8–15%).
It reflects how a society values well-being today against well-being in the future.
Economists have no consensus and no one-size-fits-all choice of rate, owing to national variations.

contested_note: The choice of social discount rate is a long-running and fierce debate among economists, sharpened by the Stern Review.
notes: Developed/developing range sentence 0cd20b7b66fe carries CITATION NEEDED.

definition.text: Frank Ramsey's formula builds the social discount rate from pure time preference plus the elasticity of marginal utility times the growth rate of consumption.

facts.text: The formula's inputs are time preference, the elasticity of marginal utility of consumption and the economic growth rate.
If future generations will be richer, a positive discount rate reflects the diminishing marginal utility of consumption.
The Stern Review let its discount rate vary with outcomes, reflecting growth and the elasticity of marginal utility, in line with Ramsey's growth model.

title: Pure time preference debate
article: Social discount rate#"Pure time preference" debates

definition.text: Pure time preference is the assumption that an experience, or a life, is intrinsically worth more the sooner it occurs, and whether society should use it is disputed.

facts.text: Philosopher Toby Ord says most philosophers think pure time preference lacks moral justification, and Frank Ramsey called it ethically indefensible.
Derek Parfit compared it to an indefensible spatial discount rate that would care less about effects per yard of distance.
Andreas Mogensen argues a positive rate can be justified by kinship, since common-sense morality lets us favour those closer to us.
Over long spans a fixed rate becomes counterintuitive: 1% would mean Tutankhamun should value one day of his life above all lives today.
When asked about the welfare of others rather than their own, most people's apparent pure time preference shrinks or vanishes.
Critics warn that weighting future generations fully can lead to a 'Pascal's mugging' conclusion that present welfare barely matters.

contested_note: Economists commonly include pure time preference, while most philosophers reject it and some defend it on kinship grounds.

title: Discounting in climate economics
article: Social discount rate#In global climate change

definition.text: The choice of discount rate for the benefits of cutting greenhouse gas emissions is a highly controversial question in climate economics.

facts.text: The Stern Review of 2006 warned that global GDP risked a 20% cut unless 1% of world GDP was invested now to reduce global warming.
Critics objected that its findings partly rested on an extremely low pure time preference rate of 0.1%.
It is a common misconception that the Stern Review used a zero discount rate: its projections used many positive rates while taking time preference near zero.
Discount rates in climate cost–benefit analysis range from zero to over 3%.
A rival model with a 3% rate declining to 1% over 300 years found carbon taxes necessary but much smaller than Stern recommended.
Under Obama the US social cost of carbon was $51/ton at a 3% discount rate; Biden proposed over $190/ton using lower rates.
The rate is usually positive because resources invested today can, on average, become more resources later.
The choice of discount rate has a large effect on any climate cost analysis: too high a rate means too little mitigation, too low a rate too much.

contested_note: Some argue giving future generations less weight is ethically indefensible, others that equal weighting yields nonsensical results.
distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

definition.text: The expected value of an uncertain quantity is the average of its possible values, each weighted by how likely it is.

facts.text: It can be read as the long-run average result of repeating the same random experiment many times, as the law of large numbers shows.
For a fair six-sided die, whose faces 1 to 6 each have probability 1/6, the expected value is 3.5.
When all outcomes are equally likely, the expected value is simply the ordinary average.
It is usually written E(X), E[X] or EX; the letter E goes back to W. A. Whitworth in 1901.
The idea arose in the mid-17th century from the problem of points: how to split stakes fairly when a game ends early.
Pascal and Fermat solved it on the principle that a future gain is worth an amount proportional to the chance of getting it.
Christiaan Huygens published the first treatise on it in 1657, often seen as the first foundation of probability theory.
In decision theory, a person choosing under incomplete information is often assumed to maximise the expected value of their utility.

definition.text: An interest rate is the interest charged or paid each period, expressed as a share of the amount lent, deposited or borrowed.

facts.text: Rates are normally quoted per year.
Total interest depends on the rate together with the principal, how often interest compounds and the length of time.
Interest rates reflect a borrower's willingness to pay for money now rather than money in the future.
Firms borrow from banks expecting the borrowed capital to earn a return greater than the interest rate.
Riskier investments such as shares and junk bonds normally have to promise higher returns than safer government bonds.
Changing interest rates raises or lowers the opportunity cost of investing for firms.
The spread is the lending rate minus the deposit rate, and it covers banks' operating costs.

definition.text: The real interest rate is the interest rate after allowing for inflation, while the nominal rate is the rate before that adjustment.

facts.text: Real rates measure what is repaid against the buying power the money had when it was lent or invested.
If inflation equals the nominal rate, the real rate is zero.
The Fisher equation links real rates, nominal rates and the inflation rate; it can be used with projected (ex ante) or historical (ex post) rates.
Lenders and borrowers accept a nominal rate made up of the real rate they require plus the inflation they expect.
Real rates can be negative when nominal rates are below inflation.

definition.text: Central banks set target interest rates as a main tool for influencing investment, inflation and unemployment.

facts.text: Central banks usually cut rates when they want more investment and consumption in the economy.
Very low rates can be risky, feeding economic bubbles in property and stock markets.
The US federal funds rate varied between about 0.25% and 19% from 1954 to 2008.
A zero interest-rate policy sets the target near zero, where conventional monetary policy struggles because market rates are hard to push below zero.

title: Negative interest rate

definition.text: A negative interest rate charges savers for holding money and has been described as a tax on holding money.

facts.text: In theory lenders will not lend below 0% when they could hold cash instead, since that guarantees a loss.
Silvio Gesell proposed negative rates in the late 19th century.
The European Central Bank from 2014 and the Bank of Japan from early 2016 used negative rates alongside quantitative easing.
During the European debt crisis some countries' government bonds sold at negative yields.

notes: Anchored to the 'Theory' subsection of 'Negative nominal or real rates'; could instead anchor to 'Interest rate#Negative nominal or real rates'.

definition.text: Liquidity preference is the tendency of people and firms to prefer holding cash or easily sold assets over harder-to-convert investments.

facts.text: It shows up as a yield gap between assets of different maturities and conversion costs.
It explains why longer-lasting assets usually have to offer higher yields.

definition.text: Present value is what a stream of expected future payments is worth as of today.

facts.text: Present value is usually below future value because money held now can earn interest, which is called the time value of money.
Put simply, a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow, since today's dollar can be invested and earn a day's interest.
If a zero-coupon $100 note payable in one year sells for $80 now, $80 is its present value.
Working out what money today will be worth later is called capitalization; the reverse, valuing future money today, is discounting.
The usual model uses compound interest, and (1 + i) to the power −n is called the present value factor.
The net present value of a stream of cash flows discounts each flow to the present and adds them up.
A risk-free interest rate is used for riskless projects; for risky ones a risk premium is added, judged from projects with similar risks.
When both timing and size of cash flows are uncertain, an expected present value approach weighs several scenarios by their probabilities.

title: Perpetuity
article: Present value#Present value of a perpetuity

definition.text: A perpetuity is a series of regular payments that continues indefinitely.

facts.text: Few such instruments actually exist.
Its present value is the limit of the annuity formula as the number of payments goes to infinity.
A perpetuity immediate pays at the end of each period and a perpetuity due at the start; their values differ by a factor of (1 + i).

definition.text: Years' purchase is the traditional way of valuing an income stream by multiplying its average expected yearly cash flow by a fixed number.

facts.text: A lease paying $10,000 a year sold at 20 years' purchase is valued at $200,000, which equals discounting in perpetuity at 5%.
Buyers of riskier income pay fewer years' purchase.
The English crown used it to set resale prices for manors seized at the Dissolution of the Monasteries in the early 16th century.

definition.text: Risk aversion is the tendency to prefer a more certain outcome to a riskier one, even when the risky option pays the same or more on average.

facts.text: A risk-averse investor may choose a bank account with a low guaranteed rate over shares that could pay more but might lose value.
Offered a sure $50 or a coin flip for $100 or nothing, a risk-averse person would accept a sure amount below $50, such as $40.
A risk-neutral person is indifferent between the bet and a sure $50; a risk-loving person takes the bet even against a sure $60.
The certainty equivalent is the smallest sure amount a person would accept instead of a gamble; it is a measure of risk aversion.
The risk premium is the gap between a gamble's expected value and its certainty equivalent, positive for the risk-averse.
In expected utility theory a person is risk-averse exactly when their utility function is concave.
On average, higher earners are less risk-averse than lower earners.

title: Arrow–Pratt measures of risk aversion

definition.text: The Arrow–Pratt measures express how risk-averse a person is from the curvature of their utility function, in absolute or relative terms.

facts.text: The more curved the utility function, the higher the risk aversion.
Absolute risk aversion is named after economists Kenneth Arrow and John W. Pratt and is built from the first and second derivatives of utility.
Relative risk aversion has no units, so it can be compared across settings; logarithmic utility gives a constant relative risk aversion of 1.
In intertemporal choice problems, relative risk aversion often cannot be separated from the elasticity of intertemporal substitution.

distinct_from: Rabin's critique of expected utility risk aversion

title: Rabin's critique of expected utility risk aversion
article: Risk aversion#Limitations of expected utility treatment of risk aversion

definition.text: Rabin's calibration theorem criticises using expected utility theory to explain risk aversion in small-stakes decisions.

facts.text: It shows that someone who always refuses a 50–50 bet to lose $100 or gain $110 would also refuse a 50–50 bet to lose $1,000 or gain any sum.
Rabin finds this implausible: small-stakes aversion from diminishing marginal utility would imply extreme aversion at large stakes.
Prospect theory answers this by judging outcomes against a reference point, usually the status quo, rather than final wealth.

contested_note: Rabin argues the expected utility account of small-stakes risk aversion is implausible; prospect theory offers an alternative.

title: Risk aversion in public policy
article: Risk aversion#Public understanding and risk in social activities

definition.text: Many government agencies have risk-averse mandates that require risks to be minimised, sometimes at the cost of the benefits of the risky activity.

facts.text: Reducing a risk has an opportunity cost: the value lost by not taking the risky action.
Laws focused on risk without weighing its benefits may misrepresent society's goals.
Risk-averse planning of schools and playgrounds often keeps children from activities they would otherwise benefit from.

distinct_from: Rabin's critique of expected utility risk aversion

definition.text: The time value of money is the idea that receiving a sum of money now is generally better than receiving the same sum later.

facts.text: Money held today can be invested to earn a return, so a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future.
It is one reason interest exists: interest compensates a depositor or lender for losing the use of their money.
It compares cash flows at different dates by converting them all to one valuation date, often called time 0.
An amount PV invested at rate i grows to PV(1 + i)^n after n periods; discounting reverses this to find present value.
The present value formula is the core formula, and the others, such as the annuity formula, are built from it.
It is weighed when judging the opportunity cost of spending rather than saving or investing.
Compound interest was used in business from the Middle Ages, and pricing annuities was a key setting for developing present-value methods.
Cost–benefit analysis adjusts all costs and benefits for the time value of money, expressing them as a net present value.

title: Future value

definition.text: Future value is what an amount invested today will be worth after a given number of periods of earning interest.

facts.text: An amount PV invested at time 0 at rate i per period is worth PV(1 + i)^n after n periods.
The factor (1 + i)^n is the accumulation factor, and (1 + i)^−n is the matching discount factor.
Present value is usually below future value because money has interest-earning potential.

notes: No page of its own in the crawl; mentioned across Time value of money, Present value and Discounting.

title: Growing perpetuity
article: Time value of money#Present value of a growing perpetuity

definition.text: A growing perpetuity is an endless stream of payments that rises at a fixed rate, valued by a simple formula when growth is below the interest rate.

facts.text: This formula is the well-known Gordon growth model used to value shares.
Few real securities grow at a fixed rate forever, but the approach is still used to value real estate, equities and other assets.

definition.text: Uncertainty describes situations where information is imperfect or unknown.

facts.text: It applies to predictions of future events, to measurements already made and to the unknown, and matters especially for decision-making.
It arises in partly observable, random, complex or changing environments, and from ignorance.
It is a state of limited knowledge in which the possible future states, their probabilities or their values cannot all be fully described.
Uncertainty can be measured only when treated as risk, by assigning probabilities to each possible outcome.
Adaptive management is an iterative way of deciding under uncertainty that aims to reduce it over time through monitoring.

definition.text: Risk is uncertainty that has been quantified: the possible outcomes have known probabilities and some of them involve losses.

facts.text: Not knowing whether it will rain tomorrow is uncertainty; giving it a probability, say from a weather forecast, quantifies the risk.
If a business event loses $100,000 when it rains and rain has a 10% chance, the risk is a 10% chance of losing $100,000.
The expected opportunity loss multiplies the chance of loss by its size, here $10,000, which suits only a risk-neutral decision-maker.
Most people would pay a premium to avoid the loss, so insurers charge more than the expected loss.
Risk differs from variability: risk concerns one uncertain future value, variability the spread of many observed values.

title: Knightian uncertainty

definition.text: Knightian uncertainty is uncertainty that cannot be measured or turned into probabilities, as distinct from measurable risk.

facts.text: Frank Knight drew the distinction in 1921, in Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit.
To Knight, risk can in principle be insured, but true uncertainty cannot.
Known risks can be insured because they have a defined probability distribution; uncertainties lack one and can lead to extreme outcomes.
Knight called those who bear uncertainty entrepreneurs, so entrepreneurship research studies how uncertainty creates opportunities.
It is named after Frank Knight, who separated risk from uncertainty in his 1921 book Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit.
Knight held that measurable uncertainty, risk proper, is so different from unmeasurable uncertainty that it is not really uncertainty at all.
The concept admits a basic limit to knowledge and an essential unpredictability of future events.
It remains largely informal: there is no single best formal system of probability and belief to represent it.

notes: Drafted from the Uncertainty page's Knightian section; the seed page itself sits in another chunk range.; Also drafted in part04 from the Uncertainty page; fold at merge.

definition.text: Radical uncertainty is uncertainty that no available means of gaining knowledge could resolve.

facts.text: John Kay and Mervyn King popularised the term in a book published in March 2020.
It differs from Knightian uncertainty in whether the uncertainty can be resolved: if research could remove it, it is not radical.

definition.text: Scientific uncertainty is often understood differently by the public than by scientists, and can be misread as ignorance or lack of consensus.

facts.text: Differences between studies caused by method can look to the public like a lack of consensus where one actually exists.
Climate change deniers followed Frank Luntz's advice to frame global warming as a matter of scientific uncertainty.
Scientific uncertainty may be managed deliberately to reach certain goals.

definition.text: Ambiguity aversion is a preference for risks whose odds are known over risks whose odds are unknown.

facts.text: It was first shown by the Ellsberg paradox: people prefer betting on an urn of 50 red and 50 black balls over one of 100 balls in an unknown mix.
Risk aversion concerns a gamble against its expected value when odds are known; ambiguity aversion concerns known odds against unknown odds.
Unlike risk aversion, mainly put down to diminishing marginal utility, ambiguity aversion has no widely accepted main cause.
It has been used to explain incomplete contracts, stock-market volatility and selective abstention in elections.
Greater ambiguity aversion raises demand for insurance, as people dislike unknown events affecting their lives and property.
Experiments suggest attitudes to ambiguity depend on context, so a measure from one setting may not predict behaviour in another.

definition.text: Maxmin expected utility is a model in which a decision-maker holds several possible probability beliefs and picks the option whose worst-case expected utility is highest.

facts.text: Gilboa and Schmeidler proposed it in 1989 as an axiomatic account of ambiguity aversion.
Someone who thinks the chance of red in the unknown Ellsberg urn lies between 0.4 and 0.6 would, under maxmin, prefer to bet on the known urn.
Schmeidler's Choquet expected utility model, which allows non-additive probabilities, includes maxmin as a special case.
A max-min social welfare function reflects an extreme uncertainty aversion by society, caring only about the worst-off.

definition.text: An annuity is a series of equal payments made at regular intervals, usually for a limited term.

facts.text: Life insurers commonly sell annuities: a person pays a lump sum or premiums in return for regular income, often for retirement.
Everyday examples include regular savings deposits, monthly mortgage payments, insurance premiums and pension payments.
Its value is expressed as a present or future value by discounting or accumulating the payments at a stated interest rate.
An annuity-immediate pays at the end of each period, like mortgage repayments; an annuity-due pays at the start, like rent.
An annuity that continues indefinitely is a perpetuity.
In medieval and early modern Europe, annuities let lenders provide credit where direct interest-bearing loans were restricted.
By the 16th and 17th centuries governments in the Dutch Republic, France and England sold annuities to raise money.

definition.text: A life annuity pays for as long as one or more named people stay alive, so the number of payments is uncertain.

facts.text: Pensions paying a regular income for life are life annuities.
By contrast, an annuity certain pays for a fixed period whatever happens to anyone's survival.
Valuing a life annuity accounts for mortality as well as interest: its actuarial present value is the expected value of the discounted payments.
Halley's 1693 work showed how a life table built from mortality data could be used to price annuities.

definition.text: Compound interest is interest earned on both the original sum and on interest already added to it.

facts.text: It differs from simple interest, where past interest is not added to the principal.
$1,000 at 5% a year grows to $1,050 after one year and $1,102.50 after two, because the second year's interest is on the new total.
The compounding frequency can be yearly, monthly, daily, continuous or not at all until maturity.
Compound interest at a constant rate gives exponential growth of capital.
Luca Pacioli's Rule of 72 (1494) says the years for money to double is roughly 72 divided by the interest rate.
Lenders charging compound interest were once condemned as the worst kind of usury under Roman law.
Garrett Hardin argued any economy based on long-term compound interest must fail, since exponential growth is impossible on a finite planet.

definition.text: Continuous compounding is the limit reached when interest is compounded ever more often, with the compounding period shrinking towards zero.

facts.text: Under continuous compounding the effective annual rate approaches an upper limit of e^r − 1.
The continuously compounded rate is called the force of interest.
It is often used because it is mathematically simpler, for example when valuing financial derivatives.
Jacob Bernoulli discovered the constant e in 1683 by studying a compound interest question.

definition.text: The effective annual rate is the total interest payable over one year divided by the principal, putting rates with different compounding on a common footing.

facts.text: Many countries require lenders and banks to disclose this annual compound rate so consumers can compare products fairly.
It goes by names such as annual equivalent rate (AER), effective annual percentage rate and annual percentage yield.
Bonds paying interest twice a year have a yearly compounded rate higher than their quoted rate.

definition.text: The cost of capital is what a company pays for its funds, both borrowed and from shareholders, or the return investors require for providing them.

facts.text: It is the minimum return investors expect, so it sets the benchmark a new project must beat.
An investment is worthwhile only if its expected return on capital exceeds the cost of capital.
It equals what the money could earn in the best alternative investment of similar risk: the opportunity cost of capital.
For projects outside a firm's core business, its usual cost of capital may be the wrong yardstick, since the risks differ.
Finding it means estimating both the cost of debt and the cost of equity, and both must look forward to expected future risk and return.
The discount rate used in financial calculations is usually set equal to the cost of capital.

title: Weighted average cost of capital
article: Cost of capital#Weighted average cost of capital

definition.text: The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) blends a firm's cost of debt and cost of equity into a single cost of capital.

facts.text: It is the minimum return a firm must earn on its assets to satisfy its lenders, owners and other capital providers, or they will invest elsewhere.
WACC can be used as the discount rate for a project's projected free cash flows.
Debt is cheaper than new equity for profitable firms because of tax advantages, but too much debt raises default risk and borrowing costs.
Management seeks the financing mix that minimises the cost of capital and so maximises the firm's value.

definition.text: The cost of equity is the return shareholders require, inferred by comparing the investment with others of similar risk.

facts.text: It is commonly computed with the capital asset pricing model: the risk-free rate plus beta times the market's risk premium.
Beta measures a security's sensitivity to movements in the market.
The market risk premium has averaged around 5% in some developed countries during the twentieth century and up to 7% in emerging markets.
The cost of debt is found by taking a risk-free bond rate matching the debt's term and adding a default premium.

definition.text: Decision theory, or the theory of rational choice, uses expected utility and probability to model how people would act rationally under uncertainty.

facts.text: It is mainly prescriptive, identifying optimal decisions for a rational agent rather than describing how people actually choose.
Its roots lie in 17th-century probability theory from Pascal and Fermat, refined by Huygens.
Daniel Bernoulli introduced expected utility in the 18th century; von Neumann and Morgenstern formalised it in the 1940s.
Choice under uncertainty is the heart of decision theory.
Allais and Ellsberg showed systematic departures from expected-utility maximisation, and Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory renewed empirical study.
Kahneman and Tversky found that losses loom larger than gains, people focus on changes rather than levels, and probability estimates are biased by anchoring.
It also covers intertemporal choice, where actions lead to outcomes at different times, such as spending a windfall now or saving it for a pension.

definition.text: Decision theory splits into a normative branch about how an ideal rational decision-maker should choose and a descriptive branch about how people actually choose.

facts.text: Applying the normative approach in practice is decision analysis, which builds tools and software to help people decide better.
Descriptive models include Tversky's elimination by aspects and Laibson's quasi-hyperbolic discounting for time-inconsistent choices.
Behavioral decision theory has drawn growing interest in recent decades.

definition.text: Heuristics are shortcuts for making a decision without working out the consequences of every option.

facts.text: They cut the thinking needed but are more prone to fallacies and errors than step-by-step reasoning.
The gambler's fallacy wrongly expects heads to be 'due' after a run of tails, though a fair coin's chance stays 0.5.
The compromise effect leads people to favour moderate options over extreme ones.

title: Limits of probabilistic decision theory

definition.text: Whether probability can be replaced by something else in decision theory is a highly controversial question.

facts.text: Defenders of probability cite Cox's justification of its axioms, de Finetti's Dutch book arguments and the complete class theorems.
Supporters of fuzzy logic, Dempster–Shafer theory and info-gap theory say probability is only one option among many.
Probabilistic rules can be sensitive to assumed probabilities, while rules such as minimax make no such assumptions and are robust.
The ludic fallacy critique holds that models of a fixed set of possibilities ignore 'unknown unknowns' that may have outsized impact.

contested_note: Advocates of probability theory and of non-probabilistic alternatives disagree on whether probability should remain the basis of decision theory.

definition.text: A discount function gives the weights an economic model places on rewards received at different times.

facts.text: With time-separable utility, total utility from a stream of consumption is the sum of each period's utility weighted by the discount function.
Exponential and hyperbolic discounting are the two most common examples.

definition.text: Discounted cash flow analysis values a security, project, company or asset by allowing for the time value of money in its expected cash flows.

facts.text: All future cash flows are estimated and discounted, usually at the cost of capital, and their sum is the net present value.
The discount rate combines the time value of money (the risk-free rate) with a risk premium for the chance the cash flows never arrive.
Run in reverse, taking a known price and solving for the rate, it gives the internal rate of return or a bond's yield.
It is widely used in investment finance, real estate development, corporate finance, actuarial science and patent valuation.
It has been used in the UK coal industry since 1801 and was first set out in modern terms by Irving Fisher (1930) and John Burr Williams (1938).
Its forecasts assume the future resembles the past, and small input changes, especially to terminal value, can swing the result greatly.
Traditional DCF counts only financial costs and benefits, leaving out environmental, social and governance performance.

definition.text: Integrated Future Value extends discounted cash flow and net present value to count the long-term value and risks of natural and social capital.

facts.text: It lets companies value investments for their long-term environmental and social returns as well as financial ones.
The social cost of carbon can be included to capture the damage to society from an investment's greenhouse gas emissions.
It supports Integrated Bottom Line decisions, which combine financial, environmental and social reporting in one balance sheet, going beyond the triple bottom line.

definition.text: Exponential discounting is a discount function in which value falls by the same proportion for each extra unit of delay.

facts.text: Total utility is the sum of each period's utility multiplied by the discount factor δ raised to the power of the time period.
The trade-off between consumption at two dates depends only on how far apart they are.
It is dynamically consistent: preferences do not change as time passes unless new information arrives.
It is the most common assumption in economics because of its simplicity, though alternatives such as hyperbolic discounting have more empirical support.
In finance, discounting is normally modelled as exponential.

definition.text: Discounted utility is how desirable a future event, such as consuming a good, looks from the present rather than when it happens.

facts.text: It is the present discounted value of future utility, smaller than the future utility for anyone who prefers sooner gratification.
The discount factor β lies between 0 and 1 and is sometimes explained as a person's patience.
Intertemporal consumption models maximise the sum of discounted utilities subject to a budget constraint on the present value of spending.
Tversky and Kahneman found people who choose 1 candy bar now over 2 tomorrow also choose 2 in 101 days over 1 in 100 days: inconsistent time preferences.

definition.text: Epstein–Zin preferences are a form of recursive utility that separates attitudes to risk from attitudes to substituting consumption over time.

facts.text: Recursive utility combines a time aggregator for preferences without uncertainty and a risk aggregator that sets the certainty equivalent of future utility.
A parameter β sets the rate of time preference and ρ sets the elasticity of intertemporal substitution, while α encodes risk aversion.
Unlike standard expected utility forms such as isoelastic utility, the elasticity of intertemporal substitution can be set independently of risk aversion.
Setting α equal to ρ gives back ordinary time-additive expected utility.

definition.text: The expected utility hypothesis holds that people choose between risky options by comparing the probability-weighted average of the utility of each outcome.

facts.text: It is a foundational assumption of mathematical economics about decisions under uncertainty, and rational choice theory builds on it.
Expected utility is the sum over outcomes of each payoff's utility times its probability.
The curve of the utility function captures risk attitude: linear for risk-neutral, convex for risk-seeking and concave for risk-averse people.
Bernoulli's version was the first formal statement of marginal utility: an extra sum is worth less to a rich person than a poor one.
Von Neumann and Morgenstern defined a rational decision-maker by four axioms: completeness, transitivity, independence and continuity.
Psychologists have found systematic violations, and behavioural finance has produced generalised theories such as prospect theory to account for them.
Such deviations are called irrational because they depend on how a problem is presented, not on its costs, rewards or probabilities.

title: St. Petersburg paradox
article: Expected utility hypothesis#The St. Petersburg paradox

definition.text: The St. Petersburg paradox is a coin-flipping game with an infinite expected payoff that people will nonetheless pay only a little to play.

facts.text: The prize doubles each time the coin lands heads, and the game ends at the first tails.
Someone caring only about expected value should pay any finite amount to play, but in reality few would pay more than $25.
Nicolaus Bernoulli described it in 1713, prompting expected utility theory as a solution.
Daniel Bernoulli's 1738 paper used it to argue that expected value theory must be normatively wrong.

title: Subjective expected utility
article: Expected utility hypothesis#Savage's subjective expected utility representation

definition.text: Subjective expected utility is Leonard Savage's framework showing that expected utility, with personal probabilities, can guide choice even when probabilities are not objectively known.

facts.text: Savage proved, from seven axioms, that expected utility can be used to make an optimal choice among acts.
Its key method is a focus on observable choices; psychology matters only as far as it changes choices.
Frank Ramsey's 1926 representation theorem was an earlier approach to subjective probability.
Savage concluded that people are neutral towards uncertainty and that observation is enough to predict the probabilities of uncertain events.

title: Preference reversal over lotteries
article: Expected utility hypothesis#Preference reversals over uncertain outcomes

definition.text: A preference reversal occurs when people value one lottery more when pricing it but choose the other when comparing them directly.

facts.text: Subjects price 'p bets' (high chance of a small prize) below '$ bets' (small chance of a big prize), yet usually pick the p bet head to head.
The effect was found in studies starting with Lichtenstein and Slovic in 1971.
Later work suggests the behaviour can fit neoclassical theory under specific assumptions.

definition.text: Inflation is a rise in the average price of goods and services measured in money, which means each unit of money buys less.

facts.text: It is measured with a price index, usually a consumer price index, and the inflation rate is the yearly percentage change in that index.
Its opposite, a fall in the general price level, is deflation.
Inflation refers to the general trend of prices, not a change in any single price.
Causes include growth in the money supply, demand shocks, supply shocks such as energy crises, interest-rate cuts and changing expectations.
High or unpredictable inflation harms an economy: it makes long-term planning hard and uncertainty about money's future value discourages saving and investment.
It shifts buying power away from people on fixed incomes, such as pensioners whose pensions are not indexed to prices.
Most economists today favour a low and steady inflation rate, a task usually given to central banks.
Since the Great Depression of the 1930s, prices have generally risen every year.

definition.text: Climateflation is inflation driven by climate change, through its effects on food production and supply chains.

facts.text: The term, first used by Isabel Schnabel of the European Central Bank, covers price rises from heat, droughts and floods that hit farm output.
In 2022–2023, climate-driven heat in Europe raised food prices by about 0.7%, adding about 0.3% to overall inflation.
The same study found warming expected by 2035 could raise these effects by 30–50%.
A related term, fossilflation, describes inflation caused by fossil fuel prices, which push up transport, food and shipping costs.

verification.title: Global warming and heat extremes to enhance inflationary pressures
verification.evidence: Finally, the 2022 extreme summer heat increased food inflation in Europe by 0.43-0.93 percentage-points which warming projected for 2035 would amplify by 30-50%.

definition.text: Inflation targeting is a monetary policy in which the central bank keeps adjusting its interest rate to steer inflation towards an official target.

facts.text: It began in New Zealand in 1990 and has spread to most developed countries.
In most OECD countries the target is about 2%.
Research suggests true inflation runs about one percentage point below the official figure, so a 2% target keeps true inflation from nearing zero or deflation.
New Zealand became the first country to adopt an official inflation target, in 1990.

title: Theories of inflation

definition.text: Economists have long debated what causes inflation, with competing theories such as the quantity theory of money and the real bills doctrine.

facts.text: Keynes argued in 1936 that wages and prices are sticky in the short run but respond gradually to swings in demand.
In the 1960s Milton Friedman's monetarism challenged this view, holding that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.
In the 1970s the link between inflation and unemployment broke down, which was eventually put down to changing inflation expectations.
Since about 2000 the common view gives roles to demand shocks, supply shocks and inflation expectations.

contested_note: Rival schools have disputed inflation's causes for centuries, from the quantity theory versus real bills to Keynesians versus monetarists.

definition.text: Insurance is protection from financial loss: for a fee, one party promises to pay another if a particular loss, damage or injury happens.

facts.text: It is a form of risk management, used mainly to guard against a loss that may or may not happen.
The buyer accepts a certain, known and fairly small loss, the premium, in exchange for the insurer's promise to pay if a covered loss occurs.
A deductible (or excess) is the amount the insured must pay out of pocket before the insurer pays a claim.
Insurance transfers the financial burden of a chance event to a bigger entity; it does not lower the chance that the event happens.
Needing an insurable interest, a real stake in the loss, is what separates insurance from gambling.
Chinese and Indian traders spread risk as early as the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC; Chinese merchants split cargo across many boats so one capsizing lost little.
Economists and consumer advocates in the United States generally see insurance as worthwhile for rare, catastrophic losses but not for likely, small ones.
Insurance can help households and societies prepare for and soften catastrophes, but it can also raise fraud and careless behaviour.

definition.text: Risk pooling is gathering money from many insured people or firms so that it can pay the losses that only some of them will suffer.

facts.text: Each member is protected for a fee, and the fee depends on how often and how badly the insured event tends to happen.
Because policies cover members of large classes, insurers can rely on the law of large numbers, under which predicted losses come close to actual losses.
Instead of joining a pool, a person or firm can self-insure by saving money for possible future losses.
Some communities, including the Amish and some Muslim groups, rely on mutual support from their community when disaster strikes rather than on insurance contracts.

definition.text: Insurability is the set of features a risk must have for private companies to be able to insure it.

facts.text: An insurable loss should be definite in time, place and cause, accidental rather than in the insured's control, and large enough to matter to the buyer.
Both the probability of loss and its cost must be at least estimable, and the premium must stay affordable relative to the cover.
Losses should ideally be independent and not catastrophic, so they do not all strike at once and bankrupt the insurer.
Limited capital constrains how much earthquake insurance, and wind insurance in hurricane zones, insurers can sell.

definition.text: An insurance premium is the price charged for cover, set to cover expected claims, costs and profit, minus what the insurer earns by investing it.

facts.text: Setting premiums, called ratemaking, is actuarial work that uses statistics and probability to estimate future claims for a given risk.
Insurers bring historical loss data to present value and compare it with premiums collected to judge whether rates are adequate.
Float is money collected as premiums but not yet paid out in claims; insurers invest it and earn income on it until claims are paid.
US property and casualty insurers lost $142.3 billion on underwriting in the five years ending 2003 but made $68.4 billion overall thanks to float.

definition.text: Reinsurance is insurance for insurance companies: another insurer agrees to carry part of a risk that the first insurer finds too large.

facts.text: The reinsurance market is dominated by a few large companies with huge reserves.
Single properties worth more than any one insurer's capital limit are shared among several insurers or syndicated into the reinsurance market.

definition.text: Property insurance protects against risks to property such as fire, theft or weather, and includes special forms for floods, earthquakes and crops.

facts.text: Crop insurance helps farmers manage losses from weather, hail, drought, frost, pests or disease.
Index-based insurance pays farmers when a modelled climate trigger, linked to a high chance of large crop loss, is exceeded and harvest losses occur.
Many US insurers do not offer flood insurance in some regions, so the federal National Flood Insurance Program acts as insurer of last resort.

definition.text: Interest is the extra money a borrower pays a lender, on top of paying back the amount borrowed, at a set rate.

facts.text: A bank customer usually pays interest to borrow, paying back more than was lent, and earns interest on savings, withdrawing more than was deposited.
Unlike a dividend, which a company shares out from profit, interest is paid at a rate fixed beforehand.
In economics the interest rate is the price of credit and acts as the cost of capital.
One explanation for interest rates usually being above zero is that loanable funds are scarce.
In the sixteenth century Martín de Azpilcueta argued that a good now is better than the same good later, so interest pays the lender for giving up spending in the meantime.
Sumerian documents from 3000 BC show systematic lending of grain and metals, and interest seems to have been well established by then.
Jacob Bernoulli is thought to have discovered the constant e by studying what happens as interest is compounded more and more often.

definition.text: Simple interest is interest worked out only on the original amount owed, without adding interest on earlier interest.

facts.text: It can be applied over periods other than a year, for example every month.
On a $2500 credit card balance at 12.99% a year applied monthly, one month's simple interest is $27.06.
Compound interest differs by also earning interest on interest already accumulated.

definition.text: The rule of 72 estimates how many years money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate in percent.

facts.text: At 6 percent a year, money doubles in about 72/6 = 12 years.
The rule gives a good indication for interest rates up to 10%.

definition.text: Market interest rates are set in markets such as the money market, bond market and banks, and each loan's rate reflects several factors.

facts.text: Lenders weigh opportunity cost, the other uses of their money, including the return from competing investments.
A lender putting off consumption wants at least enough to cover price rises from inflation; nominal interest is roughly the real rate plus inflation.
A risk premium covers the chance of default, so loans to developing countries carry higher premiums than loans to the US government.
Shorter loans usually carry less default and inflation risk, so short-term rates are often below long-term rates, an upward sloping yield curve.
Investors want a higher return on an asset that is hard to resell quickly at a fair price than on a liquid one.
Central banks strongly influence short-term rates, one of the main tools of monetary policy.

definition.text: Theories of interest are the explanations different schools of economic thought have offered for why interest exists and what sets its rate.

facts.text: Aristotle and the Scholastics held that money is by nature sterile, so it was unjust to charge for being parted from it.
In the classical theory of Mill and others, the interest rate adjusts to balance the demand for borrowing with the supply of lending.
Wicksell's 1898 Interest and Prices distinguished natural from nominal interest rates; Ohlin and Robertson later refined this into the loanable funds theory.
In Keynes's 1936 General Theory, interest is set by the demand for money, liquidity preference, against a given money supply.

title: Internal rate of return

definition.text: The internal rate of return (IRR) is the yearly rate of return at which the net present value of all of an investment's cash flows equals zero.

facts.text: It is called internal because it ignores outside factors such as the risk-free rate, inflation, the cost of capital or financial risk.
Used before the fact it estimates a future annual return; used afterwards it measures the return actually achieved.
A project whose estimated IRR exceeds the firm's cost of capital for it is profitable.
IRR measures an investment's profitability or efficiency, while net present value measures how much value it adds.
For cash flows of -123,400, then 36,200, 54,800 and 48,100 over three years, the IRR is 5.96%.
In savings and loans the IRR is also called the effective interest rate.
A project with a negative net present value is not necessarily loss-making; it means its internal rate of return is below the required rate.
The modified internal rate of return was developed to fix some problems with it and to rank investments of unequal size.

distinct_from: Problems with the internal rate of return

title: Problems with the internal rate of return
article: Internal rate of return#Problems with use

definition.text: The internal rate of return has known flaws as a decision rule, chiefly that ranking projects by it can disagree with ranking them by net present value.

facts.text: When the aim is to maximise total value, IRR should not be used to choose between mutually exclusive projects: a bigger project can have a lower IRR but a higher NPV.
Despite a strong academic preference for NPV, surveys show executives prefer IRR.
When cash flows change sign more than once, a project may have several IRRs, and it is unclear whether high or low is better.
Whether IRR hides an assumption that all cash flows are reinvested is debated: some sources say yes, others say no.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether the IRR assumes cash flows are reinvested at the IRR until the project ends.

definition.text: Intertemporal choice is the study of how people value payoffs that arrive at different times, usually simplified to now versus some future date.

facts.text: John Rae introduced the idea in 1834; Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk in 1889 and Irving Fisher in 1930 developed the model further.
Consuming something today means it cannot be consumed in the future, so choices trade present against future consumption.
Diminishing marginal utility is a key idea used to analyse intertemporal choice, along with choice under uncertainty and social welfare.
Uncertain fuel prices and high discount rates for running costs make energy-efficiency investments look riskier to many decision makers.

definition.text: The Fisher model shows how a consumer with present and future income, able to lend or borrow at an interest rate, chooses between consuming now and later.

facts.text: It assumes constant income and utility maximisation, and treats investments as generators of savings.
With present income Y(t), future income Y(t+1) and interest rate r, the most one can consume now is Y(t) + Y(t+1)/(1+r).
The most one can consume in the future is (1+r)Y(t) + Y(t+1).

definition.text: Theories of intertemporal consumption try to explain how people choose between spending and saving over the course of their lives.

facts.text: Irving Fisher and Roy Harrod first described 'hump saving', with saving highest in middle age as people prepare for retirement.
In the 1950s Modigliani and Brumberg, Ando and Friedman treated lifetime consumption as an optimisation problem, producing the life-cycle model.
The life-cycle model says consumption follows average lifetime income: the young borrow, earners save more, and retirees live off savings.
Tests have had mixed success: people under-consume early and late in life and over-consume in their peak earning years.
Proposed fixes include a bequest motive, liquidity constraints, utility that changes over time, or particular expectations about future income.
John Rae first conceived it in the 1830s and Irving Fisher expanded it in the 1930s.
The basic model has two periods, such as youth and old age.

title: Behavioural life-cycle hypothesis

definition.text: The behavioural life-cycle hypothesis says people split their wealth into separate mental accounts, current income, savings and future income, and spend differently from each.

facts.text: The share spent out of each account differs: close to all of current income, close to none of future income, and somewhere between for current assets.
These differences help explain over-consumption in peak earning years and why higher pension contributions do not cut other saving.

notes: Section-less concept described in the lead of Intertemporal consumption; passes test 5 only weakly, keep as Minor.

title: Isoelastic utility

definition.text: Isoelastic (power, or CRRA) utility is a standard formula linking utility to consumption, with one parameter, η, setting how strongly extra consumption is valued less.

facts.text: It is the only family of utility functions with constant relative risk aversion, hence the name CRRA utility.
With risk involved, η is the degree of relative risk aversion; η = 0 means risk neutrality and η = 1 gives logarithmic utility, ln c.
Under constant relative risk aversion, the share of wealth put in a risky asset does not depend on how rich one is.
The true value of η is much debated: asset prices need values up to 50 in some models, but most experiments suggest values just above 1.
Estimates include 1.5 for the United Kingdom (Groom and Maddison, 2019) and about 1.4 across 20 OECD countries (Evans, 2005).
Using six well-being surveys, Layard and colleagues (2008) found values between 1.19 and 1.34, with a combined estimate of 1.26.

contested_note: Economists disagree on the true value of η, with asset-price models needing far higher values than experiments and surveys suggest.

definition.text: A black swan event, in Nassim Nicholas Taleb's sense, is an important and inherently unpredictable event that people explain with hindsight once it has happened.

facts.text: Black swan theory holds that preparing for such events is hindered by pretending to know all the risks.
Taleb argues that Knightian risk does not exist in the real world, which instead has gradations of computable risk.

definition.text: Minimax is a decision rule that picks the option whose worst possible outcome is least bad; for gains it is called maximin, maximising the minimum gain.

facts.text: It was first formulated for zero-sum games between players and later extended to general decisions under uncertainty.
A player's maximin value is the most they can be sure of getting without knowing what the other players will do.
In two-player zero-sum games the minimax solution is the same as the Nash equilibrium.
Minimax values are central to the theory of repeated games, including the folk theorem.
It suits cases without good probability models but can overweight very unlikely, costly events.

definition.text: Minimax can guide a single decision maker facing unknown facts, treating the choice as a game against nature and minimising the worst-case loss.

facts.text: Prospecting for minerals is an example: the cost is wasted if no minerals are found but rewards are large if they are.
Unlike expected value or expected utility, it makes no assumptions about the probabilities of outcomes, so it is robust to changes in assumptions.
Extensions of this non-probabilistic approach include minimax regret and info-gap decision theory.

definition.text: In John Rawls's A Theory of Justice, maximin is the difference principle: social and economic inequalities should be arranged to benefit the least-advantaged most.

facts.text: John Harsanyi instead used the original position to argue for utilitarianism, since rational agents weigh expected outcomes rather than worst cases.

definition.text: Precautionary saving is putting aside part of one's income because future income is uncertain.

facts.text: It arises because insurance markets are incomplete, so people cannot insure against every bad future state of the economy.
People consume less now to build a reserve they can draw on if income falls, keeping consumption smooth.
Typical reasons include health risk, business risk, unavoidable expenses, possible loss of earnings, retirement and children's education.
Saving is a flow, measured per unit of time, while savings are the stock of funds accumulated at a point in time.
Numerical simulations put precautionary saving at 20 to 60 percent of all saving, though the evidence overall is mixed.
In recessions the precautionary motive strengthens, raising total saving and cutting total consumption.
Countries behave similarly: fast-growing emerging economies have built up savings, sending capital 'upstream' to rich countries.

definition.text: Prudence is the strength of a person's precautionary motive to save in the face of risk, defined by Kimball in 1990.

facts.text: Leland (1968) linked prudence to decreasing absolute risk aversion with convex marginal utility, U''' > 0, and showed even small income risks create precautionary saving.
Kimball defined absolute prudence as q = -U'''/U''; it measures the precautionary motive just as risk aversion measures the desire for insurance.

title: Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model

definition.text: The Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model, or neoclassical growth model, is a foundational model of how an economy grows over time when saving is chosen to maximise welfare.

facts.text: It builds on Frank Ramsey's 1928 work, extended by David Cass and Tjalling Koopmans in the 1960s.
Unlike the Solow–Swan model's fixed saving rate, it derives saving from a household's optimisation over time.
Ramsey framed it as a social planner maximising consumption across generations; Cass and Koopmans recast it as a market economy with a representative agent.
Future utility is discounted exponentially at a rate ρ, which must exceed population growth n for total welfare to be finite.
Consumption grows when the marginal return on capital, net of depreciation, exceeds the discount rate ρ.
The optimal path is a unique saddle path that converges on the steady state; other paths end with all saving or with capital used up.
It aims to explain long-run growth, not business cycles, and leaves out market imperfections, differing agents and shocks.
A social welfare function is maximized by choosing a consumption path, subject to a differential equation for capital per effective worker.

notes: Also drafted in another chapter; fold at the cross-chapter duplicate stage.

definition.text: The elasticity of intertemporal substitution measures how willing a person is to shift consumption between periods; it reflects how much they want to smooth consumption over time.

facts.text: It is formally the inverse of relative risk aversion: high relative risk aversion means a low elasticity and a stronger wish to smooth consumption.
With logarithmic utility the elasticity is constant at 1.

definition.text: A nominal value is measured in plain money amounts, while a real value is measured by the goods and services that money can actually buy.

facts.text: Real value allows for inflation and reflects purchasing power.
Real values are found by dividing the nominal value by the growth factor of a price index, giving values in, for example, constant 1992 dollars.
Real GDP removes inflation from growth figures to show how much an economy actually grows; nominal GDP includes inflation and is higher.
Real wages, the buying power of wages, are the after-tax nominal wage divided by the growth factor of the consumer price index.
In one example the real wage rose 20 percent, so an hour's wage bought 20% more goods in year 2 than in year 1.
Output from different regions can be compared by repricing their goods at common or average prices.

title: Price index
article: Real and nominal value#Commodity bundles, price indices and inflation

definition.text: A price index tracks the cost of a fixed sample basket of goods, a commodity bundle, relative to its cost at a base date or place.

facts.text: The index is usually set to 100 at the base date; if the bundle's price rises one percent in the first period, the index becomes 101.
The inflation rate between two dates is the change in the price index divided by its earlier value.
The consumer price index uses a bundle of goods bought by consumers; GDP uses its own GDP price index.
Indices are usually set so the base period equals 100: if prices rise 5% from a 2010 base, the 2011 index is 105.

title: Fisher equation
article: Real and nominal value#Real interest rates

definition.text: The Fisher equation says the real interest rate is approximately the nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate.

facts.text: Looking back, the ex post real rate is roughly the historical nominal rate minus inflation; looking ahead, the expected real rate is the nominal rate minus expected inflation.
Nominal interest is made up of the real rate plus inflation, among other factors such as credit risk.

definition.text: Real options valuation applies the methods used to price financial options to decisions about investing in real projects.

facts.text: A real option is the right, but not the duty, to defer, abandon, expand, stage or shrink an investment project.
Real options are most valuable when uncertainty is high and managers have room and willingness to change course.
Standard net present value treats managers as passive once money is committed, ignoring the flexibility to react to how markets turn out.
In a worked example, NPV says invest now for a gain of 1M, but waiting a year for information is worth 1.21M, so the firm should wait.
A negative NPV does not always mean a firm should not invest: opening one store and expanding later if demand is high can be worth 0.41M.
In natural resource exploration a firm can delay mining a deposit until market conditions are favourable.
Unlike financial options, the underlying project and the option itself are often not tradable.
Stewart Myers of MIT coined the term 'real option' in 1977, after Black–Scholes (1973) made financial options analysable.

definition.text: Risk neutral preferences are neither risk averse nor risk seeking: the person cares only about the expected payoff, not how uncertain it is.

facts.text: Its utility function is linear in wealth, so maximising expected utility is the same as maximising expected wealth; risk averters have concave and risk lovers convex utility.
A risk neutral investor would put everything in the asset with the highest expected yield, while a risk averse one diversifies.
The QALY model in health economics assumes, among other things, risk neutral behaviour.

definition.text: A risk premium is the extra return a person demands to accept more risk, generally the expected risky return minus the risk-free return.

facts.text: Choosing a risky share over a 3% risk-free treasury bond, an investor might demand 8%, a risk premium of 5%.
Risk premiums are larger during economic downturns and periods of heightened uncertainty.
The more risk averse a person or firm, the larger the premium they will pay to avoid a risk; it usually falls as wealth rises.
For bonds the risk premium is called the credit spread: the extra yield over a risk-free treasury bond.
Schroeder estimated stock market risk premiums of 4.83 to 7.75 percent in the UK and EU, mostly between 6.3 and 7.2 percent.
In some models, the option value of investing in invasive species quarantine or management is a risk premium.
When a multiply-resistant wheat cultivar was released in 2000, it sharply cut the risk premium farmers bore against Fusarium head blight.

title: Compensating risk premium in wages
article: Risk premium#Risk premium application in managerial economics

definition.text: Workers in riskier jobs are paid more as a risk premium, so the labour market puts a price on risk through wage differences.

facts.text: The premium rises with the risk of injury, so average wages in dangerous jobs are higher.
The risk need not be physical: higher unemployment risk is also paid for, one reason fixed-term contracts tend to pay more.

notes: Basis of hedonic wage methods used to value risk to life; check the valuation chapter for a matching entry.

definition.text: Stochastic dominance is a way of ranking risky options so that one is preferred by every decision maker in a broad class, even when their exact utility function is unknown.

facts.text: It gives only a partial order: some pairs of gambles cannot be ranked against each other.
Statewise dominance is the simplest case: one option is at least as good in every possible state, like an insurance policy with a lower premium and better cover.
A first-order dominant gamble gives at least as high a chance of getting at least x for every x, so everyone who prefers more to less chooses it.
Second-order dominance roughly means less risk with at least as high a mean; all risk-averse expected-utility maximisers prefer the dominant gamble.
Risk aversion matters only in second-order stochastic dominance.
A higher expected value does not imply dominance: in one example gamble C has a higher mean than A yet does not first-order dominate it.
The original version of prospect theory produced violations of first-order stochastic dominance.

title: Time preference

definition.text: Time preference, also called time or delay discounting, is how much more a person values getting something sooner rather than later.

facts.text: The higher the time preference, the more future returns or costs are discounted.
It shows in choices like $100 today versus $110 in a month: taking the $100 implies an annual discount rate of at least 10%.
It is captured by the discount function; the main models are exponential, hyperbolic and quasi-hyperbolic.
John Rae began the study, arguing that wealth differs across nations because of differences in saving, driven by willingness to delay gratification.
In Irving Fisher's neoclassical theory, the rate of time preference underlies the real rate of interest.
Thomas Schelling framed climate change as an intergenerational discounting problem: how to share well-being between present and future generations.
The Stern Review set δ = .1%, η = 1 and g = 1.3%, giving a 1.4% discount rate; William Nordhaus objected that this near-zero time preference drove its conclusions.
There is still no consensus on the climate discount rate; revealed environmental discount rates of countries span 1%-10%.

contested_note: Experts disagree on what discount rate to use for climate change, as the Stern–Nordhaus exchange shows.

definition.text: Real choices show patterns that a single constant discount rate cannot explain: people's discounting shifts with framing and with the kind of decision.

facts.text: Richard Thaler found that gains are discounted more than losses and small amounts more than large ones.
Discounting rises as a time interval is cut into smaller parts; Daniel Read argues this sub-additivity makes discounting look hyperbolic.
Temptation theories explain why people pay for commitment devices that remove tempting options from their future choices.

definition.text: Personal discount rates are measured either by asking people to choose between smaller-sooner and larger-later rewards, or by inferring them from real-world choices.

facts.text: Researchers vary amounts and delays to find the indifference point, where the smaller sooner and larger later rewards are valued equally.
There is still no consensus on the rate, partly because how a study asks its questions can change the result.
Energy-efficient air conditioners cost more upfront but save money later; one hedonic pricing study of such purchases found a discount rate of 13.6%.

definition.text: People discount future outcomes at different rates depending on what is at stake, such as money, health, consumable goods or the climate.

facts.text: Studies repeatedly find steeper discounting for directly consumable rewards, like food and alcohol, than for money, possibly because of temptation.
Tabi's revealed-preference study found rates from 3% for saving lives in 100 years to 29% for adaptation to prevent flooding.
Some studies find the climate is discounted differently from health and money.

definition.text: Discount rates vary between people with factors such as age, income, gender, connection to one's future self and early life stress.

facts.text: Men generally discount more steeply than women, choosing sooner rewards more often.
Feeling more connected to one's future self may make it easier to delay gratification.
A meta-analysis found early life stress predicts time preference, making people more present-focused.
Cultural traits such as individualism, uncertainty avoidance and long-term orientation may shape national differences in time preference.

definition.text: The von Neumann–Morgenstern theorem shows that rational choice under uncertainty amounts to maximising the expected value of some utility function.

facts.text: In 1947 John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern proved that anyone whose preferences meet four axioms acts as if maximising expected utility.
The four axioms are completeness, transitivity, continuity and independence.
Choices are framed as lotteries: sets of outcomes, each with a probability, the probabilities summing to one.
The theorem forms the foundation of expected utility theory, though it claims only that such a utility function exists, not that people consciously maximise it.
Risk aversion is built in automatically, since utility need not rise in step with money.
Its utilities cannot be compared or added across people, so 'total' or 'average' utility of a population is not meaningful without extra assumptions.
Lab experiments such as the Allais paradox show expected utility predicts imperfectly; most generalised theories drop or relax the independence axiom.

title: Capital asset pricing model

definition.text: The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) gives the return an asset should be expected to earn, given how much it moves with the overall market.

facts.text: It uses beta, the asset's sensitivity to non-diversifiable market risk, plus the expected market return and the risk-free return.
Required return = risk-free rate + beta × market risk premium; a beta of 1.5 means a 10% market rise brings a 15% rise in the stock.
Treynor, Sharpe, Lintner and Mossin developed it independently in the 1960s, building on Markowitz; Sharpe won the 1990 Nobel Prize for it.
Only non-diversifiable risk is rewarded, since risk specific to one asset can be diversified away.
Its required return is the discount rate for an asset's future cash flows, and it is one model used to choose discount rates in cost–benefit analysis.
Fama and French (2004) argued its failure in empirical tests makes most applications invalid, yet it stays popular for its simplicity.

contested_note: The model fails many empirical tests, and critics such as Fama and French question most of its applications.

title: Declining discount rates

definition.text: Declining discount rates start relatively high for the near future and fall over time, to reflect long-term uncertainty and ethical concerns.

facts.text: Recent literature on the social cost of carbon supports declining rather than constant discount rates.
One climate model in the Stern Review debate used a 3% social discount rate that slowly declines to 1% over 300 years.
Over long periods, people's stated time preferences become extremely hyperbolic.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

title: Quasi-option value

definition.text: Quasi-option value is the extra value of keeping future choices open when a decision's consequences may be irreversible and uncertain.

facts.text: Arrow and Fischer (1974) and Epstein (1980) showed that possible irreversible consequences create a quasi-option effect that leads even a risk-neutral society to favour flexible decisions.
It grew out of option value, which depends on uncertain future need for an asset, irreversibility or high replacement cost if it is lost, and the asset not being storable.
In climate policy, the possible irreversibility of damage to biomes and ecosystems is weighed against the irreversibility of investing in emission cuts.
Economists have analysed the precautionary principle as the interaction of irreversibility and uncertainty.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; also called the irreversibility effect.
